strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use deterministic multiscale coordinate descent, with an exact one-dimensional search along each feasible direction. At each current vector, move along a recursively constructed Haar-like contrast direction. Every finite-support lag correlation becomes a quadratic polynomial in the scalar step. Find the global minimizer of the maximum of those quadratics on the feasible step interval by enumerating their pairwise intersections, their stationary points, and the interval endpoints. Cycle through all directions, and run a small deterministic-seed multistart pool. Accept updates only when the exact evaluator score strictly decreases, retaining the supplied construction as a protected fallback.

This is materially different from the supplied epigraph SLSQP and active-lag subgradient program, and from the earlier sampled approaches: it uses no gradients, nonlinear or linear solver, smooth-max surrogate, population recombination, random uphill acceptance, or pair-exchange mesh polling. Its search directions span all zero-sum changes at multiple interval scales, and each one-dimensional minimax problem is solved by its complete polynomial candidate set rather than by a sampled step grid. This may avoid choosing a single active lag and can make coordinated coarse-to-fine changes, but any improvement is a hypothesis, not a measured result. The full problem remains nonconvex; coordinate descent can stop at a local minimum, and the plan offers no global-optimality certificate. Exact scoring and a protected feasible fallback prevent search failure from returning a worse construction.

2. Mathematical specification
For runtime length n, represent h by n real samples and set dx = 2.0/n. The feasible set is P = {h: 0 <= h[i] <= 1 for all i, sum_i h[i] = n/2}. Thus dx*sum(h)=1.

For each lag d in {-(n-1), ..., n-1}, set p=max(d,0), r=max(-d,0), and m=n-abs(d). Define q_d(h)=dx*sum_{s=0}^{m-1} h[p+s]*(1-h[r+s]). Its index in np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full') is d+n-1. The exact objective is F(h)=max_d q_d(h), equivalently max(np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n)). Include all 2*n-1 lags and their partial-overlap boundaries. Do not use circular correlation or replace the objective with an autocorrelation identity.

Construct a hierarchical set of n-1 zero-sum directions. Begin with interval [0,n). For any interval [a,b) of length L>=2, let L0=floor(L/2) and L1=L-L0. Make a vector v that is L1 on [a,a+L0), -L0 on [a+L0,b), and zero elsewhere. Its entries sum to L0*L1-L1*L0=0. Add this direction, then recursively split the left and right subintervals. This gives n-1 linearly independent directions spanning {v: sum(v)=0}. The integer entries avoid an unnecessary normalization error; their scale is handled by the step interval.

For feasible h and direction v, the permitted scalar t satisfies 0<=h[i]+t*v[i]<=1. Initialize lo=-infinity and hi=+infinity. For v[i]>0, update lo=max(lo,-h[i]/v[i]) and hi=min(hi,(1-h[i])/v[i]). For v[i]<0, update lo=max(lo,(1-h[i])/v[i]) and hi=min(hi,-h[i]/v[i]). Coordinates with v[i]=0 impose no bound. The direction has zero sum, so every point on this line preserves the mass constraint in exact arithmetic. The resulting closed interval contains zero.

Along this line, define c=dx*np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full'), b=dx*(np.correlate(v,1-h,mode='full')-np.correlate(h,v,mode='full')), and a=-dx*np.correlate(v,v,mode='full'). For each lag index k, q_k(h+t*v)=a[k]*t^2+b[k]*t+c[k]. These formulas follow by expanding the two factors h+t*v and 1-h-t*v, and they use the same lag order as the evaluator.

The line objective is the upper envelope G(t)=max_k(a[k]*t^2+b[k]*t+c[k]) on [lo,hi]. In exact arithmetic its global minimum is attained at an endpoint, at an intersection of two lag quadratics, or at a stationary point of an active quadratic. Therefore the complete candidate set is lo, hi, zero, every in-interval real root of (a[i]-a[j])*t^2+(b[i]-b[j])*t+(c[i]-c[j])=0 for i<j, and every in-interval value -b[k]/(2*a[k]) where a[k] is nonzero. Between pairwise intersections the ordering of all quadratics is fixed, so G is one quadratic there; its minimum is at a boundary or its stationary point. Identical quadratics need no intersection root. This is an exact one-dimensional search in real arithmetic, with floating-point root tolerances specified below. The original F, not the polynomial approximation or a surrogate, decides candidate acceptance and the returned score.

3. Implementation procedure
3.1. Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) at module scope and put every helper at module scope. Use NumPy and math only; no optimizer is needed. Do not use nested functions, closures, lambdas, filesystem or network I/O, printing, or parallelism. The execution environment has at most one CPU. Implement a local exact scorer rather than assuming an undocumented signature for evaluate_erdos_solution.

3.2. Determine n before search. Try to read initial_h_values from the supplied global, convert it to a float64 flattened copy, and never modify or reconstruct the global. A parent length from 1 through 999 determines n, even if its values need repair. If there is no usable-size parent, use kwargs.get('n_points') only if it converts to an exact integer in [1,999]; otherwise set n=47. Do not resample a usable parent. Convert seed to int for np.random.default_rng; on conversion or generator failure use seed 42.

Construct the protected fallback. If the parent has the selected length, finite entries, strict bounds, and mass error at most 1e-12*max(1,n), retain a copy directly. If it is finite but fails one of those feasibility conditions, pass that same vector to project_capped and use the repaired result if successful. If the parent is missing, nonfinite, or cannot be repaired, use np.full(n,0.5). The constant vector is feasible for every positive n. Keep this fallback and its freshly computed score independently of the search states. For n=1, return [0.5] and its exact score without searching.

3.3. Implement top-level is_feasible(h,n), project_capped(z,n), and exact_score(h,n). is_feasible requires exact shape (n,), finite entries, strict bounds 0<=h[i]<=1, and abs(sum(h)-n/2)<=1e-10*max(1,n). The tolerance is for mass summation only and never relaxes coordinate bounds.

project_capped jointly projects onto the box and mass constraint; never clip and then rescale. Reject wrong shape or nonfinite input. Convert to float64 and clip extreme finite input values to [-1e12,1e12]. Let target=n/2, low=min(z)-1, and high=max(z). The function S(lambda)=sum(clip(z-lambda,0,1)) is continuous and nonincreasing, with values n and 0 at these bracket endpoints. Run 100 bisection steps; at each midpoint, if S(midpoint)>target set low=midpoint, otherwise set high=midpoint. Form h=clip(z-(low+high)/2,0,1). Compute residual target-sum(h), then distribute positive residual in index order using at most 1-h[i] capacity per coordinate, or negative residual using at most h[i] capacity. Recompute the residual and make up to two more capacity-only passes for rounding. Return None unless all entries are finite, bounds are strict, and the final mass error is within the stated feasibility tolerance.

exact_score first requires is_feasible. Compute raw=np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full'); require shape (2*n-1,) and finite entries; return float(max(raw)*(2.0/n)). Return positive infinity for any invalid input or score. Use this exact score for every start, line-search candidate, global-best update, fallback comparison, and final return.

3.4. Implement top-level add_unique_start(pool,z,n,limit) and build_starts(fallback,n,rng). add_unique_start projects z with project_capped, rejects failure, and skips a candidate if its maximum absolute coordinate difference from an existing start is below 1e-8; otherwise append a copy if the limit allows. Put fallback first. In order, try its reversal, 1-fallback, the reversal of 1-fallback, a half-block vector with floor(n/2) leading ones and a neighboring 0.5 when n is odd, an alternating 0/1 vector, cosine vectors 0.5+0.35*cos(2*pi*k*i/n) for k=1 and 2, and fallback plus seeded Gaussian noise with standard deviations 0.03 and 0.10. Generate every array from n, indices, and the RNG; do not serialize parent values. Project each construction and use a pool limit of 10. If candidates duplicate or fail, keep the smaller pool rather than adding unbounded random attempts.

Score every valid start exactly. Initialize global best_h and best_score from the protected fallback, and replace them only when a feasible start improves the exact score by more than 1e-12. Store copies. Select starts in stable increasing exact-score order, but force the fallback (pool entry zero) into the selected set if it is not already there. All pool members are scored even if they are not selected for line search.

3.5. Implement top-level build_directions(n). Use an explicit interval stack so no nested recursive helper is required. Start with (0,n). Pop an interval, skip it if its length is below two, form and append the contrast vector specified in section 2, then push the right interval followed by the left interval so the resulting order is coarse-to-fine, left-to-right. The list has n-1 directions. Build and use these directions only for n<=64; their entries and zero sums are exact integers at these dimensions.

Implement top-level line_interval(h,v) using the coordinate formulas in section 2. Reject nonfinite bounds, a direction whose sum is not within 1e-12 of zero, or an interval that does not contain zero within 1e-12. A direction with width at most 1e-14 can be treated as immovable and return the current vector from the line-search helper.

Implement top-level line_coefficients(h,v,n) using the four np.correlate expressions in section 2. Require each result to have length 2*n-1 and all coefficient arrays to be finite. Return arrays a,b,c in float64. Do not build a lag-by-coordinate Jacobian.

3.6. Implement top-level append_roots(A,B,C,lo,hi,out) for the real roots of A*t^2+B*t+C=0. Set scale=max(abs(A),abs(B),abs(C),1e-300) and tol=1e-14*scale. If abs(A)<=tol, solve the linear equation only when abs(B)>tol; otherwise treat the difference as constant or identical and add no isolated root. For a genuine quadratic, compute disc=B*B-4*A*C. If disc is negative by more than 1e-13*(B*B+abs(4*A*C)+1e-300), add no roots; otherwise clamp a small negative disc to zero. Use a cancellation-resistant quadratic formula: s=sqrt(disc), q=-0.5*(B+copysign(s,B)); if q is nonzero use roots q/A and C/q, and otherwise use -B/(2*A). Append only finite roots lying within the interval up to 1e-12*max(1,abs(lo),abs(hi)), clamping such near-boundary roots to the interval. Catch overflow or invalid scalar arithmetic by omitting that root, not by aborting the search.

Implement top-level line_candidates(a,b,c,lo,hi). Start with lo, hi, and zero. Add every finite in-interval stationary value -b[k]/(2*a[k]) for nonzero a[k]. For each pair i<j of the 2*n-1 polynomials, call append_roots on their coefficient differences. Sort the resulting finite values and remove neighbors within 1e-12*max(1,abs(t)) of one another. Keep at least lo, hi, and zero. If coefficient arrays or candidates are invalid, the caller skips the direction and retains its current vector.

3.7. Implement top-level line_search(h,current_score,v,n). Obtain the feasible interval and coefficients, then the candidate values. Evaluate the polynomial upper envelope at all candidate t values in chunks of at most 256: for each chunk form a matrix of a*t*t+b*t+c and take the row maximum. Reject nonfinite predicted values. Stable-sort the predicted scores and retain the eight lowest-ranked t values, also forcing the indices for lo, hi, and zero into the exact-check set. This bounds exact correlation calls while including the real-arithmetic line minimizer, which is a minimum of the complete polynomial candidate set. For each selected t, form z=h+t*v, pass it through project_capped, and compute exact_score. Reject invalid results. Return a copy of the candidate with the smallest exact score only if it improves current_score by more than 1e-12; otherwise return a copy of h and current_score. Resolve exact ties deterministically by retaining the first candidate in the stable candidate order. Projection may move a trial slightly off the mathematical line to restore floating-point mass; the exact scorer, not the line polynomial, judges that projected vector.

3.8. Implement top-level refine_chain(start,n,directions,line_limit,best_h,best_score). Project and exactly score start; if it is unusable, return the incoming global best unchanged. Set current to the feasible start and current_score to its exact score. Process directions in a complete coarse-to-fine sweep, then in reverse order for the next sweep, alternating thereafter. Count each attempted direction against line_limit, including an immovable or failed direction. A line-search exception skips that direction. Accept only a returned vector whose exact score is lower than current_score by more than 1e-12; update current and current_score. Independently update global best_h and best_score with a copy whenever a feasible current or line candidate improves the global score by more than 1e-12. At the end of a complete sweep, reset the consecutive-stagnant-sweep count if current improved during that sweep; otherwise increment it. Stop after two consecutive complete sweeps without improvement, when line_limit is exhausted, or after a partial sweep at the budget boundary. The current chain never worsens.

For 2<=n<=64, set total line budget B=min(276,max(n-1,floor(276*(47.0/n)**2))). Use at most three chains: chain_count=min(number_of_selected_starts,3,max(1,B//(n-1))). Divide B as evenly as possible among these chains, assigning remainder lines to the first chains, and call refine_chain sequentially on each selected start while passing the current global best through every call. This gives up to three starts and two full sweeps per start at n=47. For n>64, skip the line search entirely and return the validated fallback after exact scoring; this explicit cap bounds the quadratic-root and candidate-evaluation work. For n=1, use the direct return described earlier.

3.9. Finalize with fresh checks. Project global best_h once more and recompute its exact score. Recompute the protected fallback score. Select the projected best only if it is feasible, finite-scored, and improves the fallback score by more than 1e-12; otherwise select the fallback. If projection, scoring, or search fails, preserve the fallback. Validate the selected vector again; if necessary use a freshly constructed constant vector of length n and score it. Return a float64 NumPy vector, its freshly recomputed exact score, and int(n), in that order.

4. Search choices and useful variations
Use the defaults in section 3: preserve a usable parent resolution; otherwise use a valid requested n_points or 47; accept dimensions up to 999 but run the polynomial line search only for n<=64; use at most 10 starts, up to three selected chains, a total line budget capped at 276 with the stated dimension formula, eight predicted line candidates plus the forced endpoints and zero, and a strict score-improvement threshold of 1e-12. Use seed 42 by default. These values require no preliminary experiments.

Meaningful bounded variations are a start-pool limit of 6-12, two to four optimized starts, four to sixteen exact-scored line candidates, and a line-budget cap of 180-320 at n=47 with a fixed dimension exponent between 1.7 and 2.5. A coder may change the search cap from 64 to a fixed value between 48 and 80 only if the same finite work accounting is kept. One or three consecutive stagnant sweeps are reasonable alternatives to the default two. Any such choice must be coded as a fixed bound or explicit in-program formula, not tuned outside the program. Correctness requirements are not variations: use the full linear correlation objective, joint capped-simplex feasibility, exact-score candidate acceptance, the supplied parent as the first construction when usable, and a protected fallback.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 for h, directions, coefficients, and scores. With n<=64 in the search, the direction list uses O(n^2) values (at most 63 vectors of length 64), coefficient arrays have length 2*n-1, and the pair-root list has at most two roots per polynomial pair. Evaluate predicted scores in chunks of 256, so temporary candidate-evaluation memory is O(256*n), not O(n^3). Each line requires a constant number of correlations, O(n^2) work, O(n^2) pair-root calculations, and O(n^3) scalar-envelope evaluations; the explicit line budget bounds the total. For n>64, do not build directions or root lists; compute only the fallback score. Run all work sequentially on the single CPU. Do not construct a dense lag-by-coordinate Jacobian, a pairwise quadratic model, or a larger resolution grid.

Reject nonfinite parent data when it cannot be repaired, nonfinite polynomial coefficients, invalid roots, nonfinite trials, and infeasible projected candidates. Clamp finite projection inputs before threshold arithmetic. Handle nearly linear or identical polynomial differences and slightly negative discriminants using the tolerances in section 3.6. Treat a failed exact score as infinity. Catch failures at the direction or chain boundary so they cannot erase the best candidate or fallback. All loops have explicit size, line, start, and sweep caps. If nothing improves, return the validated parent when available, otherwise the constant 0.5 vector. This local method makes no global-optimality claim.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must define top-level run(seed=42, **kwargs) and return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points). Validate parent dimensions and values before search. Use the supplied initial_h_values as the first construction when its length is usable; repair it jointly if needed, and never redefine, hard-code, serialize, or overwrite it. Honor kwargs['n_points'] only when there is no usable-size parent. Keep the selected runtime length and never silently change resolution.

Before any candidate is stored as current or best, verify exact shape, finite entries, strict 0-to-1 bounds, mass tolerance, and a finite exact score. The score calculation must be max(np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n)) over all 2*n-1 lag values. Recompute it from the selected final vector rather than returning a polynomial, stale, or solver score. Preserve the feasible fallback from initialization onward and choose it on failure, no improvement, or a tie within 1e-12. Return no printed output or external side effects. The generated program performs these checks and computations when the harness later executes it; the source response does not claim a computed bound or verified result.
